metadata.position: Postdoc Position in String Theory
metadata.description:
The University of Hamburg invites applications for a postdoc position in the field of String Compactifications, String Geometry and String Phenomenology.

The position is in the group of Timo Weigand. It is embedded into a very active international research environment which includes the Cluster of Excellence Quantum Universe, the Collaborative Research Center 1624 ``Higher structures, moduli spaces, and integrability’’ and various other research activities at University of Hamburg and DESY, in particular in the Center for Mathematical Physics (ZMP) (https://zmp.math.uni-hamburg.de) and the Wolfgang Pauli Center (https://www.wpc-hh.de). For further information see also https://unith.desy.de.
Other members of the string theory group at University of Hamburg and DESY include Gleb Arutyunov, Craig Lawrie, Elli Pomoni, Volker Schomerus, Jörg Teschner, Alexander Westphal, and Max Wiesner.

The focus of the advertised position is to investigate string theoretic and mathematical aspects of string compactifications and quantum gravity, including implications for string cosmology and string phenomenology. It also includes a small amount of teaching.

The applicants are expected to contribute to the research of the group at an internationally competitive level and to have research experience equivalent to or comparable with a doctoral degree in theoretical physics or mathematics.
The position is limited to 3 years and expected to be filled in fall 2027.

The successful applicants will become members of the Quantum Universe research school (QURS) and through this receive offers for academic training, soft skills, and career planning. Travel money will be made available at an appropriate level. Postdoctoral research associates may participate in the supervision of doctoral and Master students, in teaching, and in the organization of the Cluster via an early career council.

Applications can be submitted via the DESY platform under this web interface (indicating that you are applying with String Theory (UNI HH)) and should include a statement of research interests, CV, list of publications, as well as the names of three referees who will be asked to upload letters of recommendation. In case of technical problems, you may contact pd-app-desyt@desy.de.
The deadline for applications for this position is 15 December, 2026.

For further questions please contact:
  • Timo Weigand, timo.weigand@desy.de

metadata.position: Postdoc in machine learning applied to complex systems
metadata.description:
We invite applications for a postdoctoral researcher to apply machine learning to complex systems at industrial scale, from the design of particle physics experiments to logistics planning with industry partners. The position is based in the group of Prof. Nicola Serra at the University of Zurich, which works in close collaboration with the group of Prof. Alessio Figalli at ETH Zurich.
The successful candidate will work in one or both of the areas described below.

Particle physics experiment design
The Future Circular Collider (FCC) is a proposed next-generation collider at CERN, and its detectors are still being designed. You will use machine learning and optimisation to explore detector design choices. This includes:
  • Detector layout optimisation: choosing the geometry, granularity and material budget of FCC sub-detectors to maximise physics reach within cost limits.
  • Reinforcement learning for large designs: using RL agents to build up large designs step by step, where each choice is conditional on the ones made before. We are also exploring large language models as a master planner that sets the overall layout and coordinates the detailed design choice.
  • End-to-end optimisation: linking design parameters directly to the sensitivity of benchmark measurements.
The work is carried out within the FCC community and builds on the group's experience using AI to optimise experiments at CERN.

Industry related projects
Through our SNSF–Innosuisse BRIDGE project, the group is bringing a proprietary optimisation methodology for large discrete decision problems from the lab into industrial use. The candidate is encouraged to take an active part in it. Within the project, the same methods are applied to container shipping and complex supply chains, working directly with industry partners. Potential projects include:
  • Container yard stacking and slot allocation: deciding where each container is placed in a terminal yard to improve efficiency, together with a port operator.
  • Planning for container shipping lines: proofs of concept with major carriers on planning and allocation problems across their networks.
  • Complex supply chains: production, inventory and distribution planning across many sites and suppliers under demand uncertainty.
You will work alongside the team leading the commercialisation of these methods, with direct contact to industry partners and their operational data.

Your profile
Required:
  • A PhD in physics, computer science, applied mathematics, operations research or a related field
  • Hands-on experience with modern machine learning tools.
  • Motivation to tackle complex problems at a realistic scale, beyond simplified benchmark problems
Desirable:
  • Experience with combinatorial or discrete optimisation, graph neural networks or reinforcement learning
  • Background in experimental particle physics or detector simulation (for the FCC work)
Experience applying machine learning to complex, real-world problems
What we offer

A 1+1-year appointment, with the possibility of further extension.
  • A salary of between 92,500-102,000 per year depending on experience
  • A small, ambitious team spanning physics, mathematics and industry, with direct access to industry partners and the CERN community
Funding for travel to conferences, CERN and partner sites
How to apply
Please send a CV with publication list, a one-page statement of research interests, and the names of two or three referees to nicola.serra+postdoc-applications@uzh.ch. Applications received before 7th January will receive full consideration.
For informal enquiries, contact Prof. Nicola Serra at nicola.serra@cern.ch.

metadata.position: ERC-funded Postdoctoral Position in Perturbative QCD and Collider Phenomenology
metadata.description:
The High-Energy Theory group at the Department of Physics at TU Dortmund University expects to open a position for a Postdoctoral Researcher in Perturbative QCD and Collider Phenomenology, funded through the “PROMETHEUS” ERC Starting Grant. The project focuses on a broad range of topics in precision QCD, including parton-shower development, resummation, higher-order QCD corrections, multi-loop calculations, and collider phenomenology in the context of the PYTHIA Monte-Carlo event generator. The appointment is initially for two years with a tentative starting date in autumn 2027. The position will be based at TU Dortmund University.

Applicants are expected to hold a PhD, or expect to complete it before the start date, in Particle Physics and have prior experience in at least one of the research areas listed above. TU Dortmund University is committed to promoting diversity and equal opportunities. In accordance with applicable legal provisions, preference will be given to female applicants. Applications from suitably qualified candidates with severe disabilities are expressly encouraged.

The Department of Physics at TU Dortmund University offers a rapidly growing research environment with high international visibility and close interaction between theoretical and experimental groups. Strong collaborations exist with groups at the University of Bonn, the University of Siegen, and Forschungszentrum Jülich through the “Color meets Flavor” Cluster of Excellence. Beyond this, the group maintains a large network of national and international collaborators, including researchers at CERN, Fermilab, Lund University, the University of Jyväskylä, Monash University, the University of Cincinnati, and RWTH Aachen University.

Skills

  • ability to work in international collaborations
  • excellent writing skills, demonstrated through previous publications in peer-reviewed journals (desirable)

  • experience in the responsible and sustainable use of LLMs for research and agentic code-development workflows, see the PYTHIA LLM policy (desirable)

  • development of novel analytical and numerical resummation techniques in perturbative QCD
  • development of the APOLLO parton shower in PYTHIA
  • publication and presentation of research results
  • contribution to the supervision of PhD students

Employment will be based on a fixed-term contract according to the collective agreement for the public sector in Germany. Remuneration will be in accordance with pay scale E13 TV-L (full time, 100%), subject to personal and collective
bargaining requirements. Further information can be found at https://oeffentlicher-dienst.info.

metadata.position: Postdoctoral position in Experimental Hadron Physics
metadata.description:
Would you like to play an active role in collecting and analysing data from an exciting, innovative experiment, supported by skilled and friendly colleagues in an international environment? Would you like to work in a department that prioritises sustainable employment and offers secure, favourable working conditions? We invite you to apply for a postdoctoral position at Uppsala University.

The research conducted at the Department of Physics and Astronomy encompasses a wide range of physics topics, distributed over nine divisions. The department is located in the Ångström laboratory and employs nearly 400 people, 100 of whom are doctoral students. It offers a broad physics curriculum to undergraduate and graduate students, participation in nationally and internationally leading projects for researchers, and opportunities for partnership with industry and various outreach activities. Read more on www.uu.se/physics.

Hyperons—unstable siblings of protons and neutrons—are not only created in experiments here on Earth; they are also hypothesised to form spontaneously in the core of neutron stars. If this is the case, it would have drastic implications for the fate of neutron stars. The fact that massive neutron stars nevertheless exist could potentially be explained by the strong force—which governs the creation of hyperons and their interactions with protons and neutrons—possessing properties that remain unknown to us. Through this new project, we will investigate this force by conducting novel hyperon experiments.
Our research group is internationally recognised for its pioneering studies on hyperons. We have long been involved in the BESIII experiment in China, the PANDA/HADES experiments in Germany, and the Belle II experiment in Japan. To systematically investigate hyperon interactions, we are now also joining the HYPS collaboration, which is currently collecting data at the SPring-8 facility in Japan. The research group is part of the Nuclear Physics Division at Uppsala University and is actively committed to fostering an inclusive work environment where employees and students can grow and develop. We encourage personal initiative and active participation in shaping the department’s activities. We offer career support for young researchers, and our many international collaborations provide access to a large professional network.

Duties
This postdoctoral position involves active participation in the HYPS experiment at SPring-8. Data collection will take place during the first half of 2027; the initial task will be an extended research visit at SPring-8, lasting approximately two months, to assist with the experiment and receive training in the analysis software. Subsequently, the postdoctoral researcher will work on data analysis at Uppsala University. Toward the end of the project, the postdoctoral researcher will also participate in the planning and preparation of new experiments. The postdoctoral researcher will work alongside a professor, a senior researcher, and a doctoral student who will be recruited for the project.
Responsibilities also include giving presentations at meetings and conferences, both within Sweden and abroad (primarily in Japan). Furthermore, the postdoc is expected to contribute to the writing of research papers and assist with the supervision of students.

Requirements
A doctoral degree in physics, or a foreign degree deemed equivalent to a doctoral degree in physics. The degree must have been obtained no later than the time the employment decision is made. Priority will be given to candidates who completed their degree no more than three years before the application deadline. Under special circumstances, the degree may have been completed earlier. Such circumstances include leave due to illness, parental leave, or positions of trust within trade unions, etc. The specific duties require a solid background in hadron physics and data analysis. The candidate must be capable of working independently while also possessing strong collaborative skills. Excellent oral and written proficiency in English is required.
Additional qualifications
Experience working with hyperon physics and practical experience with data acquisition at small- or large-scale experimental facilities are considered an advantage. Furthermore, skills in writing scientific papers and experience in supervising students is valuable.
The application must contain: CV, copies of relevant grades and degrees, a copy of or a link to the doctoral thesis, a list of publications explaining the applicant's contributions, a list of references (e.g. former supervisors) and other documents that the applicant wishes to attach. In addition, we request a two-page statement of the applicant's research interests - what the applicant’s previous experience as well as how this can be applied within the framework of this postdoctoral position.

Several postdoctoral positions will become available in the Theoretical Physics (CFT and QFT) group at the University of Pisa.

Successful candidates will join a research program -- funded by a FIS Advanced Grant from the Italian Ministry for Research -- on Quantum Field Theory and Conformal Field Theory, with a focus on modern analytical and numerical approaches to strongly coupled quantum systems. The group’s core research interests include, but are not limited to:
  • Conformal Field Theory and bootstrap techniques (analytical and numerical)
  • Quantum Field Theory at strong coupling
  • Scattering amplitudes, positivity bounds, and consistency conditions
  • Applications to both high-energy physics and condensed matter systems
The appointments are expected to be for two years, with the possibility of extension, and offer a competitive net salary by international standards. Candidates must hold (or be close to completion of) a Ph.D. in Physics. The preferred starting date is Fall 2027, although other starting dates may be considered.

Research environment:
The Physics Department at the University of Pisa is large and active, with a wide range of research areas, including QFT, lattice QCD, statistical physics and fundamental interactions (website). The group already counts 3 postdoc and 2 PhD students, and will further expand in the next few years.

Pisa also hosts a local INFN section and the Scuola Normale Superiore, further enhancing opportunities for scientific interaction and collaboration. In addition, the Galileo Galilei Institute (GGI) in Florence—well known for its advanced schools and international workshops—is located approximately one hour away.

Candidates are encouraged to express their interest by completing the online form .
In addition, three recommendation letters (in pdf format) should be sent directly by three established scientists to apply.cftmap@gmail.com with the name of the candidate in the subject of the email.

metadata.position: Single Ion Capture and Imaging to Determine the Majorana Nature of the Neutrino
metadata.description:
Is the neutrino its own antiparticle? Answering this could explain why the Universe is made of matter rather than nothing, and would reveal physics at energy scales far beyond the reach of any collider. This project develops a new way to ask the question: searching for neutrinoless double electron capture at the single ion level. In this ultra-rare nuclear process, ³⁶Ar transmutes into sulphur (or ⁷⁸Kr into selenium), and the decay leaves behind just one chemically distinct ion in the gas. Our concept, CODECS, aims to capture that single ion, identify it and image it. This would make an effectively background-free search possible, with sensitivity an order of magnitude beyond current limits. It could also produce the first observation of the standard-model two-neutrino mode in argon.

The project involves development of one of the key technologies at the heart of this scheme: moving single ions over surfaces through dense gas and watching them arrive, one by one. Ions will be swept across microfabricated radiofrequency “carpets”, which are fine-pitch electrode arrays. These use travelling-wave RF fields to levitate ions and carry them to a millimetre-scale collection point. There they meet a monolayer of molecular sensors that light up when they capture the target ion. Working with the National Graphene Institute, we will design and produce photonic integrated chips containing nanofabricated 5×5 cm carpets and integrated microscopy systems, and characterise their transport efficiency at pressures up to 5 bar. This will then be combined with a single ion source, to show that individual ions created in the gas can be delivered, captured and imaged, enabling a powerful new technology in neutrino physics.

The project sits where particle physics, ion trapping, microfabrication and optical microscopy meet. It builds on our group’s demonstration of imaging individual ions in high-pressure xenon, and you will work closely with synthetic chemists and international collaborators. We welcome applicants with a background in physics, engineering or physical chemistry who want to build instruments at the interdisciplinary frontier of particle and nuclear physics, and quantum sensing.

metadata.position: Absolute, spatially resolved, in-situ quantification of low tritium concentrations using REMPI spectroscopy.
metadata.description:
State-specific optical detection of hydrogen and its isotopologues is a pressing need for both fusion engineering, fundamental tritium science, and experiments that aim to measure the neutrino mass. Applications include analyzing material absorption and permeation, studying the composition of exhaust streams, profiling tritium beams, probing the dynamics of stored vapors, monitoring supposedly non-tritiated volumes. All of these need in situ, spatially resolved sensing of very low concentrations of atomic and molecular tritium - a problem that is only partially solved.

This project will advance a powerful modality of hydrogen isotopologue quantification, not previously applied to tritium: resonantly enhanced multi-photon ionization (REMPI) spectroscopy. REMPI uses intense, narrow-band, UV laser beams to initiate a multi-step ionization of atoms and molecules, with ions subsequently accelerated and detected electromagnetically. REMPI is both species- and state-specific, allowing for separation of signals from H, D, T, H2, T2, HT, DT, and all other isotopologues. It has fine spatial resolution, providing a signal only at the laser focus (typically <1 mm3), enabling detailed spatial mapping. Most importantly, the REMPI efficiency is close to unity, giving it an extremely low limit of detection (tens of atoms per mm3) and an absolutely predicted signal normalization. REMPI’s optical efficiency significantly outperforms competing modalities such as laser Raman spectroscopy, and its absolute detection efficiency is not only a sensing virtue but also provides a clean benchmark against which other tools can be calibrated.

This project will demonstrate REMPI for absolute spatial mapping of tritium-rich beams and vapors with world-leading precision. Technical challenges include: 1) Internal electrical detection of individual or small, countable numbers of ions using tritium compatible materials; 2) access of optical paths to active volumes through secondary and tertiary containment; 3) extraction of a small tritium signal from a much larger background of other species, and control of systematic uncertainties in quantification. These problems are all surmountable, and this project will resolve them, resulting in the first demonstration of spatially quantitative REMPI, applied to tritium.

The successful candidate will work with Professor Ben Jones, Chair of Applied Quantum Technologies whose work focuses on tritium beams and their microphysics and detection via quantum sensors; Professor Phil Edmondson, Chair in Tritium Science & Technology, an expert in tritium emanation and permeation studies; and Dr Leonie Hawkins, who is developing a new optical test beam system for tritium studies, to be operated locally at the University of Manchester at low tritium flux and ultimately integrated into tritium systems the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology for high-activity studies. The work will involve both hands-on system development and operation, modeling and analysis, ultimately yielding the first demonstration and quantitative assessment of tritium-specific REMPI spectroscopy.

metadata.position: PhD position in AI-based Newtonian-Noise mitigation for the Einstein Telescope
metadata.description:
The Experimental Particle and Astroparticle Physics Group at the University of Siegen invites applications for a doctoral researcher position in

AI-based real-time Newtonian-noise mitigation for the Einstein Telescope.

The Einstein Telescope is a planned third-generation gravitational-wave observatory designed to extend the observable frequency range down to a few hertz. At these frequencies, Newtonian noise — the direct gravitational coupling of the test masses to seismic density fluctuations in the surrounding ground — is expected to be a major sensitivity limitation and cannot be reduced by mechanical isolation.

The successful candidate will develop machine-learning methods to reconstruct and suppress Newtonian noise using multichannel measurements from seismic sensor arrays. A central objective of the project is to implement these algorithms on field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), enabling deterministic, continuous, and low-latency processing.

The project combines gravitational-wave instrumentation, multichannel signal processing, machine learning, and FPGA-based computing. The work will include the development and evaluation of suitable AI architectures, benchmarking against established approaches such as Wiener filtering, hardware-aware optimisation, and validation using a real-time FPGA demonstrator.

The Experimental Particle Physics Group in Siegen has strong expertise in detector development, FPGA-based real-time processing, and machine learning for scientific instrumentation. Siegen is also part of the Intelligent Hardware Lab (IHL) of the Cluster of Excellence “Color meets Flavor”, which is co-led from within the group and provides additional expertise in AI-enabled electronics and intelligent hardware systems.

Applicants should hold, or be close to completing, a master’s degree in physics, electrical engineering, computer engineering, computer science, or a related field. Good programming skills in Python and/or C++ are expected. Experience in machine learning, digital signal processing, FPGA development, VHDL/Verilog, or time-series analysis is advantageous, although expertise in all of these areas is not required.

The successful candidate will join the Experimental Particle Physics Group at the University of Siegen and collaborate with researchers working on the Einstein Telescope.
Participation in international collaboration meetings, workshops, and conferences is foreseen.

The position is available immediately; a later starting date can be arranged. The intended duration of the PhD project is three years. The salary will be based on the German public-sector salary scale TV-L E13, at the 2/3 level.

To apply, please send the following documents as a single PDF file to Prof. Dr. Markus Cristinziani at markus.cristinziani@uni-siegen.de by 11 December 2026:

* a motivation letter;
* a curriculum vitae;
* degree certificates and academic transcripts;
* the names and contact details of two academic referees;
* a link to the Master’s thesis and to relevant software, machine-learning, or FPGA projects, if available.

Further information is available at:

https://www.hep.physik.uni-siegen.de/
https://einsteintelescope.eu/

The University of Siegen is an equal-opportunity employer. Applications from women are particularly encouraged. Applicants with disabilities will be given preferential consideration if equally qualified.
